After months of hard work, we crossed an important marker in the Ekonomi MADANI reform agenda. The implementation of BUDI MADANI RON95 (BUDI95) is the result of a carefully considered approach to subsidy targeting that balances the people's welfare with fiscal responsibility.

The reform is straightforward: ALL Malaysians continue to enjoy subsidized fuel at RM1.99 per liter - even lower than today's RM2.05. What changes is that non-citizens and corporate users pay market rate, ensuring subsidies reach those they were intended for.

This measured approach considered the best accessibility with seamless implementation across 4,000+ stations nationwide using MyKad verification. It considered sufficient allocation for 99% of Malaysians with 300-litres per month by crunching data from the Department of Statistics. The outcome from this is expected to be between RM2.5 to 4 billion annual savings that can be redirected to programs that benefit the rakyat.

The Government took time to ensure fairness in this reform. Rather than rushing into blanket price increases, or complicated targeted cash back assistance, we chose a path that protects Malaysian families while still addressing fiscal sustainability. The success of our diesel subsidy targeting - which exceeded savings projections from RM4 billion to over RM7 billion annually, demonstrates not only that we can do this with some clear-headed thinking, but that we must do this - to sustain our economic future. 

This is responsible governance in action. Every ringgit saved from better-targeted subsidies can support education, healthcare, infrastructure, and be directed towards assistance like STR and SARA programs. 

The phased rollout begins September 27 with our armed forces and the police, followed by STR recipients on September 28, and full implementation for all Malaysians on September 30.

BUDI95 represents another step toward sustainable growth built on sound fiscal foundations. When subsidies reach their intended recipients and government resources are optimized, we create space for the strategic investments Malaysia needs to achieve high-income status.

🚗💳 Malaysia rolls out Budi95: Targeted Petrol Subsidy at RM1.99/litre

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has unveiled Budi95, a new targeted subsidy programme offering RON95 petrol at RM1.99/litre for eligible Malaysians starting Sept 30.

Key highlights:
✅ No income cap — all citizens with a valid driving licence qualify
✅ Verification via MyKad or petrol station apps (e.g. Setel, CaltexGO)
⛽300L/month cap (with additional allocation for e-hailing drivers)
❌ Foreigners will pay the market price (~RM2.60/litre)

The rollout begins in phases:
📍Sept 27 – Police & Military
📍Sept 28 – Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah recipients
📍Sept 30 – All eligible Malaysians

This move aims to make fuel subsidies more efficient and targeted, ensuring better fiscal responsibility without burdening the rakyat.

Instead of a typical corporate dashboard, I went with a neo-brutalist approach 😎😎 bold colors, high contrast, intentionally raw visuals.

• Live news feed for real-world context behind each price movement
• Designed to be accessible for non-technical users, not just analysts

With a 300-litre monthly quota, that’s roughly 7–8 full tanks.

More than enough for a typical household that drives daily — work, school runs, errands and all that.

But the real win here is that the subsidy now goes directly to Malaysians who actually need it —

and in the process, the government could save between RM2.5 billion and RM4 billion every year.

That’s what good governance looks like — small changes that quietly make a big difference.

Let's talk about Malaysia's favourite alphabet soup: B40, M40, T20.

Here's the thing — a dual-income family in KL earning RM14,000, juggling a mortgage, two kids, ageing parents, and a car loan that feels like a second marriage… is officially "T20."

Congratulations. You're "wealthy."

The framework has three quiet problems:

🔹 It's purely statistical. Being in the top 20% doesn't mean you can comfortably afford groceries — it just means 80% earn less than you.

🔹 It's geographically blind. RM8,000 in Kuala Lumpur ≠ RM8,000 in Kelantan. Yet the bracket treats them as twins.

🔹 It ignores wealth, debt, and dependents. A debt-free retiree and a sandwich-generation parent supporting 5 people sit in the same box.

Then comes BUDI95. Fiscally, rationalising a RM20B blanket subsidy makes sense. But using RM12,000 as the line between "needs help" and "doing fine" creates a cliff-edge so steep, earning RM100 more could cost you thousands in subsidies. That's not policy — that's a penalty for productivity.

A fairer path forward:
✅ A multi-dimensional index — factoring location, dependents, debt, and life stage 
✅ Graduated withdrawal instead of cliff-edge cut-offs 
✅ Redefine "wealthy" — the genuinely affluent are T5/T10, not the squeezed upper-middle 
✅ Update thresholds every 2 years, not every 5

The T20 label as shorthand for "can afford unsubsidised fuel" is lazy policymaking. Malaysians deserve a framework that reflects real lives — not just neat percentiles.

Because being classified as "rich" shouldn't feel like an inside joke.

Malaysia’s fuel subsidies helped cushion living costs for decades, but they also allowed structural inefficiencies to survive far longer than they should have.

Cheap fuel became a political tool as much as an economic policy. It reduced the urgency to improve public transport, strengthen supply chain efficiency, raise productivity, or address leakages and middle-layer inefficiencies in the economy.

Now, when subsidies are reduced, the real weakness becomes visible immediately — rising food prices, higher logistics costs, and pressure on ordinary households that still depend heavily on road transport.

The uncomfortable reality is that subsidies did not solve the problem. They merely delayed the need to fix it.
